newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN FOES SWAP OLIVE BRANCHES, UNREST GOES ON.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN FOES SWAP OLIVE BRANCHES, UNREST GOES ON.

text.p: Bulgaria's government and opposition each gave ground after ten days of unrest demanding early elections, but remained too far apart to defuse angry street protests just yet.

Anti-government unions, students and others, impoverished by a near-collapse of the Bulgarian economy, planned new rallies and strikes on Thursday despite clear moves towards negotiations between the ruling Socialists and their opponents.

Demonstrators appeared to be relishing the challenge of dreaming up novel forms of protest. Some dumped garbage before parliament on Wednesday as a sign of contempt at the "red trash" in charge, while cavalcades of horn-blowing taxi drivers halted traffic in town centres nationwide.
Oil refinery workers threatened they might down tools in one workplace "for every student beaten by police", after weekend clashes around the parliament building left at least 196 injured.

Even the highly-paid and traditionally pro-Socialist workers of the Kozloduy nuclear plant, which provides 40 percent of the country's electricity, planned a protest march on Thursday. Staff at Kozloduy are banned by law from striking.
President-elect Petar Stoyanov, soon to be empowered to call for the formation of any new government, warned the ex-communist Socialists that failure to compromise would only make things worse.
The Socialists on Wednesday "blinked first" in their confrontation with the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) by suggesting polls before the end of this year -- a year ahead of schedule.
A few hours later the opposition softened its previously uncompromising anti-government line.
"From this moment we begin negotiations with the Socialists," Ivan Kostov, leader of the Union of Democratic Forces, said after discussions among opposition leaders.
But he attached conditions, including that no new Socialist government be formed under the present parliament -- implying parliamentary polls be held earlier than the government offer.
President-elect Stoyanov, due to be sworn in on Sunday, urged both sides to reach a solution fast.
"If a consensus is not reached, I will act according to my constitutional duties and I will hand the mandate to the (Socialist) BSP and its coalition partners," he said.
"But it is my duty to warn them that if that happens, the crisis is going to be even worse and the people are not going to go back to their homes."
A spokesman for the main opposition union Podkrepa said miners, steelworkers, dockers and staff at weapons plants in the central town of Sopot staged one-hour strikes on Wednesday.

Union leaders insist they are reluctant to inflict more damage on a crumbling economy and will call full strikes only as a last resort, but said on Wednesday they wanted to hear a date for elections within two or three days.
Inflation is more than 300 percent a year and the lev currency has plunged to nearly 700 to the dollar from 70 a year ago. Most salaries are worth only a few dollars a month.
Quick formation of a new cabinet is seen as vital to secure a new funding agreement with the IMF and avert default on Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.
The Socialists won power in free elections in 1994 but Bulgaria's relatively smooth transition to democracy has been marred since by economic failure. Market reform programmes exist mainly on paper.

"We will be here as long as it takes because we are not fighting a political party, we are fighting misery and starvation," elderly demonstrator Kiril Georgiev said in Sofia. "Pensioners like me have only one hope, and that's change."
"I want those people out of power," said jobless Vladimir Velkov. "We are not evil people and we are going to forgive but I want just once in history to hear them admit their guilt."

Sofia students marched on Wednesday with "wanted" posters of outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov, accusing him of "crimes against the Bulgarian nation", and banners saying "Game over" and "Death to communism".
Elsewhere, protesters briefly blocked the road to the Danube port of Rousse with burning tyres.
The opposition is boycotting parliament, but 123 deputies from the Socialists and small parties attended its first session since protesters ransacked the building on Friday.

Repaired and cleared of debris, it was surrounded by riot police who have cordoned it off since the clashes, triggered by the Socialists' refusal to vote on an opposition motion calling for early elections.
